hazards.abt-drive-low-air: You went to pull away with the low-air warning still on. Below the warning the system may not have enough air for a full stop, and at the pop-out pressure the spring brakes apply wherever you are — including a lane of traffic. You move when the air is built and the warning is out.
hazards.abt-manual-slack: You went to wind the automatic slack adjuster by hand to shorten a long pushrod stroke. An automatic adjuster that needs manual adjustment is telling you it — or the brake behind it — has failed; winding it in hides the fault until the brake fades on a grade. Out-of-adjustment brakes are written up for a mechanic.
hazards.abt-no-chock-release: You went to release the parking brakes before the wheels were chocked. The static leak test is done with the brakes released, on a yard that is never quite level; an unchocked truck with its brakes off rolls, and the driver is looking at a gauge, not out of the windshield.
hazards.abt-spring-chamber: You went to open up the spring brake chamber to look at the leak. The spring inside a brake chamber is compressed with enough force to kill; chambers are caged and serviced only by a trained mechanic, and a driver's job is to find the leak and write it up, never to take one apart.

interrupts.alert: A loud bang and a roar of air behind the cab: the trailer emergency glad-hand has blown off and the gauge is falling fast, the low-air buzzer sounding.
interrupts.missNote: You kept watching the needle while the system emptied. In the yard the spring brakes will eventually slam on by themselves; on the road, the same blown line is a trailer that brakes itself hard in traffic while the driver is still trying to work out what the noise was.
interrupts.why: A blown line empties the system in seconds. Pulling the parking brake valve applies the spring brakes on purpose, now, instead of letting the falling pressure apply them for you with the truck in an unknown state. Then the test stops and the line is fixed.
interrupts.wrongNote: It is the yellow parking brake valve. The air is going, and the brakes should be set by you, not by the pressure running out.

interrupts.alert: A yard worker has ducked between the tractor and the trailer to look at the air lines, right where the rig would pinch if it moved.
interrupts.cue: Warn them and keep your foot where it is.
interrupts.missNote: You carried on with someone between the units and did not warn them. People working between a tractor and trailer are killed when the rig moves even a foot; the horn and a hand signal are how both of you know where the other is.
interrupts.why: The space between tractor and trailer is where people are crushed when a rig moves unexpectedly — a released brake, a truck rolling on a slope, a driver who did not know anyone was there. The horn tells the worker you are in the cab and the rig is live; your foot stays on the brake until they are out.
interrupts.wrongNote: It is the horn. Someone is standing in the pinch point between the tractor and trailer.

lateNotes.abt-brake-pedal: The applied leak test comes after the static one, with the brakes released and the air back at governor cut-out.
lateNotes.abt-dvir: The report is written once the whole check is done, so every number and every leak is on it.
lateNotes.abt-yellow-knob: The parking brakes are released for the leak test only after the chock is in and the air is built.

name: Air Brake Test

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Read the order of the check and the figures for a combination vehicle before you start.
steps.prompt: Read the order of the check and the figures for a combination vehicle before you start.
steps.title: Read the brake check card
steps.why: The in-cab air brake check is a sequence with numbers attached: how fast the air builds, where the governor cuts out, how much air the system may lose in a minute released and applied, when the warning must come on and when the valves must pop. A driver who knows the figures before starting reads each gauge against them, instead of watching a needle move and deciding it looks fine.

steps.cue: Carry the chock to the drive tandem and set it snug against the tire.

drag.missNote: Not against the tire — set the chock snug to the drive tread, in front of the wheel.

steps.prompt: Carry the chock to the drive tandem and set it snug against the tire.
steps.title: Chock the drive wheels
steps.why: The air brake check releases the brakes on purpose. On a yard that is never quite level, a truck with its brakes off and a driver watching a gauge rolls, slowly and quietly, into whatever is behind it. The chock is what lets the brakes be released safely, and it goes in before any valve is touched.

steps.cue: Hold a fast idle and time the rise on the gauge through the build range.
steps.holdBreakNote: Engine speed out of band — hold a steady fast idle so the build time means something.
steps.prompt: Hold a fast idle and time the rise on the gauge through the build range.
steps.title: Build air at fast idle and time it
steps.why: The rate the air builds is the health check for the compressor and the tanks. Driver manuals give a figure for a dual air system: from 85 to 100 psi in about 45 seconds at fast idle. Slower than that and the compressor is worn or the system is leaking faster than it fills — and a system that cannot keep up in the yard will not keep up on a mountain grade.

steps.cue: Watch the needle climb and commit at the pressure where the compressor cuts out.

gauge.label: CUT-OUT PSI
gauge.missNote: That is not the cut-out point — watch for the needle to stop and the compressor to unload.

steps.prompt: Watch the needle climb and commit at the pressure where the compressor cuts out.
steps.title: Read the governor cut-out
steps.why: The governor stops the compressor pumping at a set pressure, commonly around 125 psi on a truck, and starts it again when the pressure falls. A governor that cuts out too low leaves the system short of air for repeated stops; one that never cuts out drives the pressure up until the safety valve blows. You hear the change in the compressor and see the needle stop at the same moment.

steps.cue: Shut the engine down, then turn the key back to ON so the gauges and warning stay live.
steps.prompt: Shut the engine down, then turn the key back to ON so the gauges and warning stay live.
steps.title: Engine off, key back on
steps.why: The leak tests are done with the engine off so the compressor cannot hide a leak by topping the tanks up. The key goes back to ON because the low-air warning and the gauges run on it; with the key off, you are watching a dead dash and the warning you are about to test cannot sound.

steps.cue: Push in the yellow parking brake valve and the red trailer air supply valve, so the whole combination is released.
steps.prompt: Push in the yellow parking brake valve and the red trailer air supply valve, so the whole combination is released.
steps.title: Release the brakes
steps.why: The static leak test measures the system with the brakes off and the lines charged, so both valves go in: the yellow releases the parking brakes, the red charges the trailer and releases its spring brakes. Releasing only the tractor tests half the system, and the trailer's lines and chambers are where many leaks live.

steps.cue: Brakes released, engine off: watch the gauge for one minute and keep the loss inside the manual's figure.
steps.holdBreakNote: You lost the watch — keep your eyes on the needle and the clock for the whole minute.
steps.prompt: Brakes released, engine off: watch the gauge for one minute and keep the loss inside the manual's figure.
steps.title: Watch the static leak for a minute
steps.why: Driver manuals allow a combination vehicle to lose no more than 3 psi in a minute with the brakes released and the engine off. More than that is a leak big enough to matter on the road, where the compressor is also feeding every brake application. The minute is timed, not guessed, because a slow leak looks like a still needle for the first twenty seconds.

steps.cue: Build back to cut-out if you need to, then hold the brake pedal fully applied for one minute and watch the gauge.
steps.holdBreakNote: Your foot came off the pedal. Hold it fully applied for the whole minute.
steps.prompt: Build back to cut-out if you need to, then hold the brake pedal fully applied for one minute and watch the gauge.
steps.title: Hold the applied leak for a minute
steps.why: With the pedal held down the air is in every brake chamber, and leaks in the chambers, hoses and valves show up that a released test cannot find. After the first drop as the chambers fill, the manual allows a combination to lose no more than 4 psi in the minute. A foot that eases off partway makes the test meaningless, so the pedal is held firm and still.

steps.cue: Fan the brake pedal to drain the air: the low-air warning must come on before 60 psi, then the valves must pop out.

itemNames.abt-knob-pop: valves pop out between 20 and 45 psi

steps.outOfOrderNote: Warning first, then the pop-out — the warning has to come on while there is still air to stop with.
steps.prompt: Fan the brake pedal to drain the air: the low-air warning must come on before 60 psi, then the valves must pop out.
steps.title: Fan down to the warning and the pop-out
steps.why: The low-air warning exists to tell a driver there is trouble while there is still air to stop on; the manual expects it to come on before the pressure falls below 60 psi, and 49 CFR 393 requires the truck to have one. Fanning on down, the parking and trailer valves should pop out in the band the manual gives, commonly between 20 and 45 psi, applying the spring brakes on their own. Both are safety systems you only see work when you test them.

steps.cue: Open each tank drain and look at what comes out. Find what needs writing up.

itemNames.abt-sludge-tank: the oily sludge from the wet tank

itemNotes.abt-drain-cable: The pull cable for this tank's drain has snapped at the valve. A tank that cannot be drained fills with water, and water in the air system freezes in the lines.
itemNotes.abt-sludge-tank: The wet tank blew out oily, milky water. Oil in the tanks means the compressor is passing oil — it gums valves and freezes in winter. It goes on the report.

steps.prompt: Open each tank drain and look at what comes out. Find what needs writing up.
steps.title: Drain the tanks and read what comes out
steps.why: Compressed air carries moisture and a trace of oil, and both collect in the tanks. Draining them daily keeps water out of the valves, where it corrodes seals in summer and freezes solid in winter. What comes out tells you about the compressor, and a drain you cannot operate is a tank quietly filling with water.

steps.cue: Air back up, chock pulled: move forward slowly and apply the service brake firmly.
steps.prompt: Air back up, chock pulled: move forward slowly and apply the service brake firmly.
steps.title: Feel the service brakes at walking speed
steps.why: The last check is the one that matters on the road: does the truck stop, straight, when the pedal goes down. At walking speed a firm application should stop the combination without pulling to one side or a delayed response. A pull or a soft pedal found here costs a work order; found at highway speed it costs the lane.

steps.cue: With the brakes applied and the engine off, walk the rig and find every leak by ear.

itemNames.abt-leak-chamber: the hiss at the brake chamber
itemNames.abt-leak-drain: the drain valve left cracked open
itemNames.abt-leak-gladhand: the hiss at the glad-hand seal

itemNotes.abt-leak-chamber: A steady hiss from this brake chamber with the brakes applied — a leaking diaphragm. It goes to a mechanic; nobody opens a chamber at the roadside.
itemNotes.abt-leak-drain: This drain valve was left cracked open after draining. It is the cheapest leak to fix and the most embarrassing to be put out of service for.
itemNotes.abt-leak-gladhand: The rubber seal in this glad-hand is cracked and hissing. A few dollars of seal is the difference between a trailer that holds air and one that sets its brakes on a ramp.

steps.prompt: With the brakes applied and the engine off, walk the rig and find every leak by ear.
steps.title: Walk the rig and listen for leaks
steps.why: A leak the gauge says is within limits still has a location, and it only gets bigger. Walking the rig with the brakes applied and the yard quiet lets you hear leaks at glad-hands, chambers, hoses and valves. The CVSA out-of-service criteria take a truck off the road for audible air leaks at brake components, so an inspector will hear them too.

steps.cue: Tell the shop about the chamber, the glad-hand and the compressor oil, tell dispatch the truck is held, and say how you are.
steps.prompt: Tell the shop about the chamber, the glad-hand and the compressor oil, tell dispatch the truck is held, and say how you are.
steps.title: Check in with the shop and dispatch
steps.why: The shop can only schedule the chamber and the compressor if it hears about them, and dispatch can only find another truck if it knows this one is held. The check-in is also where a new driver says the blown glad-hand rattled them — a close call that is talked through is one that makes the next driver faster and calmer, not one that gets quietly carried.

steps.cue: Record the build time, cut-out, both leak rates, warning and pop-out pressures and every leak you found, then sign.
steps.prompt: Record the build time, cut-out, both leak rates, warning and pop-out pressures and every leak you found, then sign.
steps.title: Write the numbers in the inspection report
steps.why: 49 CFR 396 asks a driver to report defects that would affect safe operation, and a brake check without numbers is a claim, not a record. Writing down each figure against the manual's limit means the mechanic knows what to look for, the next driver knows what was found, and a pattern — a leak rate creeping up week by week — can be seen before it becomes a failure.
